sections.content: You know the *futuro simple* from A2 Unit 19, and *deber* and *haber de* + infinitive from B2 Unit 26. In a rule, regulation or contract the future does not predict. It commands. *Los socios abonarán la cuota* does not mean "the members will probably pay": it means "the members are to pay". The rule speaks to the reader as a group and in the third person, and nobody is addressed as *tú*. To make the duty explicit, a text uses *deberán* + infinitive; to make it solemn, *habrán de* + infinitive. Permission and ban follow the same pattern: *podrán* allows, *no podrán* forbids.

sections.title: What a rule can say
rows: Los socios abonarán la cuota antes del día cinco.
Members are to pay the fee before the fifth. (the future as a command)
Los socios deberán abonar la cuota.
Members must pay the fee. (an explicit duty)
Los socios habrán de abonar la cuota.
Members are to pay the fee. (formal, solemn duty)
Los socios podrán usar las herramientas comunes.
Members may use the shared tools. (permission)
Los socios no podrán ceder su parcela.
Members may not hand over their plot. (ban)

items.spanish: Los socios abonarán la cuota en enero.
items.english: Members are to pay the fee in January.

items.spanish: La junta deberá reunirse una vez al año.
items.english: The board must meet once a year.

items.spanish: Los socios habrán de cumplir el reglamento.
items.english: Members are to comply with the regulation.

items.spanish: Los socios no podrán ceder su parcela a nadie.
items.english: Members may not hand their plot over to anyone.

sections.content: English uses "shall" or "must" for rules, and the plain future for predictions. Spanish has only the future for both, so read the text type, not the form: in a notice or a regulation, *abonarán* is an order. Keep *deber* for duties: *deberán de abonar* reads as a guess ("they will probably pay"), and careful writers avoid it for rules. And never drop the *de* of *haber de*: *habrán de abonar*, not *habrán abonar*.
